title.en: Right Speech: Communication for a Flourishing Monastic Community

speaker: Pra Joshua Vajira Panyo
language_note: This talk was written and given in English. There is no Thai translation yet.
_source_note: Written by Pra Joshua Vajira Panyo and given freely. Published exactly as he wrote it, at his request — the wording, spelling and punctuation are his own. Not for sale.

paragraphs.en: I’ve recognized that communication often seems like a small issue amongst individuals or groups of individuals, yet a small issue left unaddressed can lead to big problems. It is a bit like the Broken Window Theory. A small problem that gets overlooked can become a major source of conflict within a monastic community and create much bigger problems later on.

I’ve seen this happen in families and businesses that eventually broke down and lost their good name. All that was worked hard for and planned came to a halt, went sideways, backwards, or crumbled completely, instead of moving purposely and intentionally forwards in the way that was meant to be.
It is a terrible tragedy and very sad indeed to see wasted potential.
The Buddha gives us a clear solution through Right Speech and the training of wholesome conduct.

In MN 58, the Buddha teaches Prince Abhaya about speech that is true, beneficial, connected with the good, and spoken at the appropriate time. The Buddha explains that he speaks this way because he has compassion for living beings. (SuttaCentral)

AN 5.198 gives five qualities of well-spoken speech: it is spoken at the right time, it is true, it is gentle or affectionate, it is beneficial, and it is spoken with a mind of goodwill. (SuttaCentral)
So before speaking, we can ask ourselves:
Is it true?
Is it beneficial?
Is this the right time?
Can it be spoken with kindness?
And what is the state of my mind while I am speaking?
We should avoid speech that is false, divisive, harsh, or idle. Rather than criticising, condemning, or complaining, we practise mettā and compassion.
Rather than trying to win arguments, we listen carefully and seek understanding.
Rather than focusing only on what we want, we consider the needs and perspective of others.
The Buddha’s teaching gives us a very practical standard. Being truthful alone is not enough. Our speech also needs wisdom, purpose, appropriate timing, kindness, and goodwill.

Sometimes the truth needs to be spoken even when it is difficult to hear. MN 58 shows that the Buddha did not simply avoid speech because someone could dislike hearing it. He considered whether the speech was true, beneficial, and appropriate to the time. (SuttaCentral)
This is important within a monastic community.
Right Speech does not mean keeping quiet whenever there is a problem.
Right Speech means addressing problems with mindfulness, compassion, honesty, and wisdom.

The Buddha also encouraged us to recognise wholesome qualities in one another. Sincere appreciation creates harmony, while humility and willingness to acknowledge our own mistakes prevent resentment from growing.
A flourishing Saṅgha therefore requires more than good intentions. We must train ourselves in mindfulness, patience, listening, loving-kindness, honesty, and Right Speech.
This training begins in ordinary daily situations.
When another monk says something that annoys us, we watch the mind before answering.
When a misunderstanding arises, we seek clarification rather than immediately forming a judgment.
When something needs correcting, we speak with kindness and at the appropriate time.
When we make a mistake, we acknowledge it.
When another person does something wholesome, we recognise it and express sincere appreciation.
When anger arises, we do not allow angry speech to become another cause of suffering.
This is Dhamma practice.

When monks speak truthfully, kindly, and at the appropriate time, listen with patience, forgive mistakes, and seek understanding rather than victory, communication becomes a cause of harmony rather than conflict.
The goal is not simply to communicate better.
The goal is to use communication as part of the path: reducing anger, strengthening mettā, preserving harmony, and supporting the welfare of the Saṅgha.
Every conversation becomes an opportunity to practise.
Every difficult conversation becomes an opportunity to practise patience.
Every misunderstanding becomes an opportunity to practise wisdom.
Every opportunity to speak becomes an opportunity to practise Right Speech.
In this way, our words become part of our Dhamma practice, and our Dhamma practice becomes a cause for the flourishing of the Saṅgha.
